senses.gloss:
Vārāhī
(‘boar-faced goddess’)
------------------------------------------
Durgāsaptaśatī, the well-known work of the शक्ति-cult, describes Saptamātṛkas (8.13-21), the seven aspects of the Divine मोथेर्, which are the Śaktis (female forms) of the seven deities like शिव, विष्णु, ब्रह्मा and इन्द्र. वाराही is counted among them as the fifth. She is the शक्ति of वराहावतार (Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन्) of विष्णु.
She is boar-faced, is dark in complexion and has four or six arms. On the right side she exhibits the varadamudrā (bestowal of boons), and holds दण्ड (club) as also asi (sword). On the left she shows the abhayamudrā (gesture of protection) and carries carma (shield) and pātra (bowl). Her वाहन or mount may be either an elephant or a buffalo.
Sometimes, several varieties of वाराही such as Mahāvārāhī, स्वप्न-वाराही, Dhūmravārāhī and so on are mentioned in tāntrik works. They are usually invoked in black magical rites.
See SAPTAMĀTṚKĀS.

vārakarīs
(‘those who keep fixed times’)
------------------------------------------
Paṇḍharāpura (or पण्ढर्पुर्) is a well-known and extremely popular place of पिल्ग्रिमगे (in the Maharashtra State). The main deity of this place is Viṭṭhala or Viṭhobā or पाण्डुरङ्ग (a form of Lord कृष्ण).
The pilgrims who visit this temple are of two types: the वारकरीस् (or vārkarīs) and others.
The former visit the temple regularly whereas the latter occasionally.
The वारकरीस्, again, are of two categories: those who attend every month and those who visit twice a year (on आषाढ-śukla-एकादशी [eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of आषाढ, usually in July] and Kārttika-śukla-एकादशी [eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, generally in November]).
The वारकरीस् have to observe certain rules which are binding. They are: carrying a rosary of तुलसी beads (tulasīmālā), giving up ड़्लेस्ह्-एअतिन्ग्, observing a fast on एकादशी days, carrying a flag of ochre-coloured cloth, to speak the truth and never cheat.
These rules and the very tradition of the sect have socially levelled the adherents to a great extent.
Incidentally, it may be mentioned that a similar group of devotees of राम belonging to the sect of Samartha Rāmadās, came to be known as dhārakarīs.

Varuṇapraghāsa
------------------------------------------
This is one of the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् listed under the चातुर्मास्य group.
Varuṇa is the chief deity to whom yavas (barley grains) are offered.
It needs two आहवनीय fires. Apart from the four chief priests, there will be a fifth one, pratiprasthātṛ, an assistant to the अध्वर्यु.
Offering materials are mainly yava and rice. Two figurines—one of a ram and the other of an ewe—prepared out of barley flour, are also offered into the fire.
Viṣṇukrama—four steps with appropriate mantras taken by the sacrificer—is an important part of this rite.

vārttā
(‘means of living’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu tradition divides the śāstras—authoritative texts of religion and culture—into four broad groups: trayī (the वेदस्), आन्वीक्षिकी (logic), वार्त्ता (economics and politics) and दण्डनीति (statecraft).
Vārttā, the third, is directly related to the production and distribution of wealth. It is specially assigned to the vaiśyas and they are to be trained to become experts in it.
The following are the occupations listed under it: agriculture, rearing of cattle, trade, mining and any other vocation that produces wealth and goods.

Varṇa
------------------------------------------
The ancient Hindu scriptures have divided the society into four varṇas or groups viz., ब्राह्मणस्, kṣattriyas, vaiśyas and शूद्रस्.
This division was based upon the allocation of duties and responsibilities as per their nature and nurture. (Bhagavad-gītā 18.41-44).
The ब्राह्मणस् were the custodians of knowledge. They had to learn and teach, not only spiritual wisdom, but also other branches of sciences, and arts. They were priests, preceptors and preachers. Being the custodians of the intellectual and spiritual heritage of the race, they had to guide the rulers of the land, expound and administer laws as also assist in carrying out the legislative policies.
The kṣattriyas governed the State and performed its executive functions. It was their duty as custodians of social power, to protect the society from external aggression and maintain internal law and order.
The vaiśyas generated and wielded economic power through agriculture, trade, dairy-farming and manufacture of goods.
The शूद्रस् who were not capable of independent judgement or initiative on an adequate scale, merely assisted in the discharge of essential functions by contributing manual labour.
In national calamities or emergencies change of work was permitted.
The वर्ण system gradually got fossilised into the जाति (caste) system.
The word वर्ण has two more senses: colour and letter of the alphabet.
See also CASTE SYSTEM.

varṇasaṅkara
(‘intermixing of varṇas or castes’)
------------------------------------------
Though the leaders of the Hindu society, especially the king and the ब्राह्मणस्, were very particular in preserving the purity of the वर्ण system, mixing up did take place giving rise to several subcastes and their offshoots. This mixing up (i.e., a person of one वर्ण marrying a person of another वर्ण and having children by that union) was called वर्णसङ्कर or intermixing of varṇas. This was considered bad for the society. Though अनुलोम marriages were tolerated and प्रतिलोम marriages (See ANULOMA.) were frowned upon, वर्णसङ्कर could not be prevented. Even by the time of the Mahābhārata वर्णसङ्कर had already taken place to a large extent.
It was the duty of the king to see that purity of the वर्ण-आश्रम-धर्म (or system) was kept up and punishment awarded to the transgressors (vide गौतम Dharmasūtras 11.9 and 10).

Vardhamāna Mahāvīra
(599-527 B. C.)
------------------------------------------
Jainism, one of the great religions of the world, considers 24 Tīrthaṅkaras (holy men) as its founders. Of them the last two—Pārśvanātha (circa 800 B. C.) and वर्धमान महावीर (599-527 B. C.)—are historical personalities.
Vardhamāna महावीर was born at Vaiśālī (identified with the village Basarh in the Muzaffarpur district of Bihar) to the king Siddhārtha and the queen Triśalā. During his early years, he got good एदुचतिओन् including the use of weapons of war. He led a pure life and served his parents well. In his 30th year, he renounced the world and started practising severe austerities, to realise the Truth. He attained enlightenment in his 42nd year. Thereafter, he roamed about the country—mostly in the Bihar area—preaching his doctrines and making disciples. He passed away in his 72nd year at Pāvā (the modern town of Pāvāpurī near Patna).
It was he who started the sect of Nirgranthas (those who are free from all fetters), same as Digambaras.
To the four supreme commands of पार्श्वनाथ, he added a fifth. These five are: अहिṁसा (non-injury); सत्य (truth); अस्तेय (non-stealing); अपरिग्रह (non-acceptance of gifts); and ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy).
His chief contribution was the popularisation of the principle of अहिṁसा. On its basis he elaborated an ethical code for householders and मोन्क्स्. By peaceful proselytisation, he admitted all aspirants irrespective of caste or sex. In his 30 years of ministration he had won a large number of followers, both मोन्क्स् and householders.
He also left behind a well-organised religious Order, through the efforts of which अहिṁसा became firmly established as a rule of life, even among those who did not join his Order. His followers gradually spread all over the country.
According to his philosophy it is कर्म, which is the deed of the सोउल्, that is responsible for bondage. It is a material forming a subtle bond of extremely refined kārmic matter which keeps the सोउल् confined. It is by purging the सोउल् of this कर्म, by following the commandments, that one can get लिबेरतिओन्.
Vardhamāna महावीर was a senior contemporary of बुद्ध (557-477 B. C.).
See also JAINISM and PĀRŚVANĀTHA.

Varavaramuni
------------------------------------------
Maṇavāḷa Māmuni (A. D. 1370-1443) was also known as वरवरमुनि. See MAṆAVĀḶA MĀMUNI and ŚRĪVAIṢṆVISM.

varṇāśramadharma
(‘duties of varṇas and āśramas’)
------------------------------------------
In the ancient and medieval Hindu scriptures as also religious treatises, the word ‘dharma’ is generally interpreted as वर्ण-आश्रम-धर्म, duties and responsibilities of the various varṇas and āśramas. See VARṆA and ĀŚRAMA for details.

Vararuci
------------------------------------------
There seem to be quite a few persons of this name.
The श्रौतसूत्रस् of गोभिल was also known as the Puṣpasūtras. According to some scholars, it had a South Indian recension known as Phulusūtras, attri-buted to वररुचि, either as the author or as the editor.
There was one वररुचि among the ‘Navaratnas’ (or Nine Jewels), well-known scholars, in the court of the king Vikramā-ditya.
Kātyāyana, the grammarian who composed the vārttika (explanatory notes) on the sutras of पाणिनि (4th century B. C.?) was also known as वररुचि.
The earliest grammar of the प्राकृत् language, the Prākṛtaprakāśa, was the work of a वररुचि.
However very little is known about these Vararucis.

Varāhapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
Listed as the twelfth among the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, the Varāhapurāṇa is a Vaiṣṇava work. It was taught by Varāha (third इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु) to भूदेवी (Mother Earth). The extant texts have 217 or 218 chapters, the total number of verses being around 10,000, though some पुराणस् like the Matsya mention it as 24,000. Six chapters are entirely in prose. It probably took the present shape before the tenth century A. D.
It deals with a number of stories and gives detailed accounts of vratas (religious rites) and tīrthas (places of पिल्ग्रिमगे). It also deals with several topics normally dealt with in the धर्मशास्त्रस् such as śrāddha (obsequial rites), prāyaścittas (expiations), दान (giving gifts), images and their worship, narakas (hells) and so on.
Verses from this work have been extensively quoted in the dharmaśāstra treatises.
See also PURĀṆAS.

Varāhāvatāra
------------------------------------------
Varāhāvatāra (Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन्) is the third in the series of दशावतारस् of Mahaviṣṇu in which the Lord killed the demon हिरण्याक्ष and lifted the earth out of the flood waters in which it had been submerged.
See also DAŚĀVATĀRAS.

Varāhopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor उपनिषद्स् belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and assigned to the group of योग उपनिषद्स्.
It has 263 mantras, mostly in anuṣṭubh verses, spread over five chapters. It was taught by Lord Varāha to the sage भृगु. The last two chapters were taught by the sage Ṛbhu to Nidāgha.
A brief summary of these may now be presented here:
First Chapter (17 verses)
Pleased by the तपस् (austerities) of the sage भृगु, Lord Varāha (an इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) appears before him and offers any boon he likes. भृगु asks only for ब्रह्मविद्या or knowledge of ब्रह्मन् that liberates.
The Lord, after narrating a long list of tattvas (fundamental principles of च्रेअतिओन्) advocates that भक्ति or devotion to God alone can give मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्.
Second Chapter (83 verses)
The topics discussed in this chapter are: साधनचतुष्टय (four preliminary disciplines); true nature of the आत्मन् as चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and bliss; realised सोउल् becoming one with ब्रह्मन्; he is free from the bondages of कर्म; meditation on God (Varāha) leads to dissolution of thoughts; other sādhanas leading to brahmabhāva or becoming ब्रह्मन्.
Third Chapter (30 verses)
While declaring that परमात्मन् is Sat-cit-आनन्द (existence-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्-bliss), the means of attaining him is भक्ति or devotion to him and nothing else. This is stressed here.
Fourth Chapter (12 paras and 44 verses)
This is divided into two sections, the ब्राह्मण and the मन्त्र. It has been taught by the sage Ṛbhu to the enquirer Nidāgha.
The ब्राह्मण has 12 sections in prose and the मन्त्र, 44 verses.
The first section describes seven bhūmikās or stages of development of wisdom such as śubhecchā (good desire) vicāraṇā (inquiry) and so on.
The first three stages are associated with the mumukṣu (the seeker). The yogis associated with the fourth, the fifth, the sixth and the seventh are called brahma-vid, brahmavidvara, brahmavidvarīyān and brahmavidvariṣṭha. They are the four kinds of jīvanmuktas (liberated even while living).
The second section gives a detailed description of all the stages. It also describes the characteristics of the jīvanmukta. The sages शुक and वामदेव are projected as jīvanmuktas of two types.
Fifth Chapter (77 verses)
This chapter deals with various aspects of the practice of योग. Some of them are: the eight aṅgas or steps of योग; bandhas (methods of controlling the prāṇic energy); चक्रस् (psychic centres); nāḍīs (nerve current passages); जप of प्रणव (oṅkāra) to remove obstacles and quite a few other technical details.
It ends with a phalaśruti, eulogy of the Upaniṣad, the study and practice of which results in जीवन्मुक्ति.

Varamahālakṣmīvrata
------------------------------------------
This is a regional vrata (religious festival) for women, commonly performed in South India, especially in Karnataka.
It is observed on a Friday prior to Śrāvaṇa Pūrṇimā. Only married women whose husbands are living, are entitled to do this. Worship of महालक्ष्मी, the goddess of wealth and prosperity, invoked in a कलश established on a मण्डल (sacred diagram) is the main item. A doraka (thread) is also offered in पूजा and later worn on the right hand. Gifts to other married women should be done at the end. As usual, the health and longevity of the husband, progeny and wealth are the results assured by this vrata.

Vārṣagaṇya
------------------------------------------
The साङ्ख्य दर्शन or Sāṅkhya philosophy, one of the six well-known Hindu philosophical systems, is based on the Sāṅkhyakārikā of ईश्वरकृष्ण (5th century A. D.). However, this systematic treatise and others of a similar nature are said to have been modelled on an earlier work called Ṣaṣṭitantra (philosophy of sixty basic principles) attributed to वार्षगण्य who probably lived sometime during the period A. D. 100-300. Whether he was its author or had only compiled it from various earlier sources, is not known.
Practically nothing has been dis-covered about his life and works.

Vāruṇī
------------------------------------------
Vāruṇī means liquor or an intoxicating drink. Hence, वारुणी represents the goddess that presides over it.
Vāruṇī is also the name of one of the queens of the deity वरुण. She is known as गौरी too.
The deity वारुणी, also known by other names such as Amṛteśvarī and Sudhāmālinī, is described by the works on इचोनोग्रफ्य् as a goddess with four arms holding a cup of liquor, a bowl of cooked meat, a bejewelled jar and a blue lotus. She is surrounded by a host of śaktis or feminine spirits.
As an associate of the goddess ललिता she is described as the controller of the fleet of boats.

Varadarāja
------------------------------------------
Varadarāja, the king among the bestowers of boons, is another aspect of Lord विष्णु which is very popular. Also known as Karivarada, it represents that aspect of the Lord responsible for saving Gajendra, the elephant king, from the death-clutches of the crocodile.
The temple of Śrī वरदराज at Kāncīpuram in South India, is one of the most important and famous विष्णु temples.

Varivasyārahasya
(‘secret of upāsanā or meditation’)
------------------------------------------
This is a short but well-known work of the शाक्त school of the तन्त्रस्. It was composed by Bhāskararāya Makhin (17th-18th Century). It has 167 kārikās (brief sentences) divided into two aṁśas or sections (53 + 114 = 167). The author himself has written a detailed gloss on it.
The work expounds in detail the philosophy behind the श्रीचक्र and the Pañcadaśākṣarī मन्त्र by connecting them with the various tattvas or principles taught in the तन्त्रस्.
It is an esoteric and a highly complicated work.
See मन्त्र">PAÑCADAŚĀKṢARĪMANTRA and ŚRĪCAKRA.

Varāhamihira
(A. D. 505-587)
------------------------------------------
Hindu science of अस्त्रोनोम्य् has its roots in ज्यौतिष, considered one of the six वेदाङ्गस् (limbs of the वेदस्). Scholars feel that it dates back to at least 1400 B. C.
The Sūryasiddhānta, believed to be a revealed work, is the earliest treatise available on this subject. It was thoroughly revised by वराहमिहिर, a great name among the Hindu astronomers.
Varāhamihira was the son of Ādityadāsa of Kapitthaka or Avantikā.
Practically nothing is known about him. Tradition describes him as one of the ‘Navaratnas’ or ‘Nine-jewels’ of scholars adorning the court of the king विक्रमादित्य.
His well-known works are: Bṛha-jjātaka, Bṛhatsaṁhitā, Laghujātaka and Pañcasiddhāntika.
He was both an astronomer and an astrologer.
In the Pañcasiddhāntika he enunciates the astronomical principles embodied in the works of ancient scholars like Pailiśa, Romaka, वसिष्ठ and Brahma.
The first two treatises enlisted above are on अस्त्रोलोग्य्. Incidentally they also furnish some geographical data.
Varāhamihira was the first astro-nomer to furnish a revised version of the Hindu चलेन्दर्, after calculating the precession of the equinoxes from the period of the preparation of the earlier Sūryasiddhānta.
He has employed śūnya or ज़ेरो as a positive numerical symbol.

Varuṇa
------------------------------------------
Varuṇa ‘the one who encompasses the whole world,’ is one of the oldest Vedic deities. Maybe he is the personification of the sky; but he is also associated with clouds and water, rivers and ocean. He is sometimes clubbed with मित्र and praised (Mitrāvaruṇa).
Varuṇa is the king of the universe and lives in the highest world. His knowledge and power are unlimited. He has thousand eyes and oversees the whole world. Hence he is the lord of the moral law. He punishes those who transgress this law but forgives them out of compassion if they repent and pray. By activating वायु, the lord of the wind, he sustains life by giving rain and crops.
Though वरुण was the chief deity in the beginning, he seems to have yielded his place later on to इन्द्र and प्रजापति.
In the subsequent mythological literature वरुण is described as the presiding deity of the western quarter and as the lord of oceans, water and aquatic animals. In some of the temples he is depicted as riding on a crocodile. In two of his four arms he holds the serpent and the noose (pāśa). Sometimes he is pictured as riding a chariot drawn by seven swans and holding the lotus, the noose, the conch and a vessel of gems in the four hands. There is an umbrella over his head.
